note: Every module below is status:draft. Flip to 'published' only after you have checked it against the cited source and local guideline.

modules.title: Hyperkalaemia: don't miss the ECG, don't under-dose the calcium

bullets.text: Severe hyperkalaemia is usually defined as K+ 6.5 mmol/L or above
ECG progression: peaked T waves, then broad QRS, then sine wave, then arrest
A normal ECG does not exclude it — sensitivity is poor
Calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL IV to stabilise the myocardium. Repeat if no ECG change
Insulin 10 units with dextrose 25 g IV. Monitor glucose for at least 6 hours
Then treat the cause and consider potassium removal. Discuss with renal early

deep_dive.heading: Sequence at the bedside
steps: Attach continuous cardiac monitoring before anything else
12-lead ECG and repeat venous gas to confirm — rule out a haemolysed sample
Calcium first if there are ECG changes: it buys time but does not lower K+
Insulin-dextrose next: onset roughly 15 minutes, peak effect at about 1 hour
Salbutamol nebulisers are an adjunct only, never a substitute
Ask why: AKI, drugs (ACEi, ARB, spironolactone, trimethoprim), rhabdomyolysis, Addison's

quiz.question: A 72-year-old on ramipril and spironolactone is weak. K+ 7.1 mmol/L, ECG shows a broad QRS. Which drug goes in first?
options: Insulin 10 units IV
Calcium gluconate IV
Salbutamol 10 mg nebulised
Sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol IV
quiz.explanation: Calcium stabilises the myocardium and is the first drug when there are ECG changes. It does not lower K+ — follow it immediately with insulin and dextrose.

source.title: Treatment of acute hyperkalaemia in adults

modules.title: Occlusion MI: the patterns that don't meet STEMI criteria

bullets.text: Millimetre STEMI criteria miss a substantial minority of acute occlusions
Posterior MI: horizontal ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves
Do posterior leads V7 to V9 — only 0.5 mm elevation is needed there
De Winter pattern: upsloping ST depression with tall symmetrical T waves
Modified Sgarbossa criteria apply when there is LBBB or a paced rhythm
Ongoing pain with a dynamic ECG warrants a cardiology conversation, not a wait

deep_dive.heading: What to do with the suspicion
points: Repeat the ECG every 10 to 15 minutes while pain continues
Compare with any previous ECG before calling a change new
Record posterior and right-sided leads and label them clearly on the trace
Escalate on the pattern and the story, not on whether the millimetres are met

quiz.question: Chest pain, ECG shows 2 mm horizontal ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves and upright T waves. Next step?
options: Treat as NSTEMI and admit
Record posterior leads V7 to V9
Give thrombolysis
Repeat troponin at 3 hours and reassess
quiz.explanation: This is the mirror image of posterior injury. Posterior leads confirm it, and only 0.5 mm of elevation in V7 to V9 is required.

source.title: ECG library — posterior myocardial infarction

modules.title: Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline early, and what to do when it doesn't work

bullets.text: Adult dose: adrenaline 500 micrograms IM into the anterolateral thigh
Repeat every 5 minutes if there is no improvement
Refractory means no improvement after two appropriate IM doses
Refractory anaphylaxis needs an adrenaline infusion and expert help
Lay the patient flat — sitting or standing up has been linked to arrest
Steroids are no longer routinely recommended in the initial treatment

deep_dive.heading: If two IM doses have not worked
steps: Call for senior and critical care help now
Start an adrenaline infusion per your local protocol and stop repeat IM dosing
Give a rapid IV fluid bolus — distributive shock is often profound
Consider whether this is airway obstruction requiring immediate intervention
Observe after recovery: biphasic reactions occur, so follow local observation periods
Serial mast cell tryptase, adrenaline autoinjector, and an allergy referral before discharge

quiz.question: An adult with anaphylaxis has had two doses of IM adrenaline 5 minutes apart with no improvement. What is the next step?
options: A third IM dose
IV adrenaline bolus 1 mg
Start an adrenaline infusion and call for critical care help
Give hydrocortisone 200 mg IV
quiz.explanation: This is refractory anaphylaxis. Guidance moves to an adrenaline infusion with expert help rather than continued repeat IM dosing.

source.title: Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis: guidelines for healthcare providers

modules.title: Adult DKA: the four things that go wrong in the first two hours

bullets.text: Fixed rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour — weight-based, not a standard rate
Continue long-acting basal insulin. Stopping it causes rebound ketosis
Add glucose-containing fluid once blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L
Potassium falls fast — check it early and replace within the infusion
Resolution is ketone and pH based, not glucose based
Euglycaemic DKA happens on SGLT2 inhibitors — check ketones despite normal glucose

deep_dive.heading: Traps worth naming at handover
points: Do not withhold potassium replacement waiting for a formal lab result if the gas shows it
Bicarbonate is not routine and can worsen intracellular acidosis
A rising glucose on treatment usually means the infusion is not actually running
Look for the precipitant: infection, missed insulin, MI, pregnancy, drugs

quiz.question: A patient in DKA on an SGLT2 inhibitor has a blood glucose of 9 mmol/L. Which statement is correct?
options: DKA is excluded by the normal glucose
Euglycaemic DKA is recognised and ketones must be checked
Insulin should be withheld until glucose exceeds 14 mmol/L
Only sodium bicarbonate will correct the acidosis
quiz.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose. Diagnosis rests on ketones and acidosis, and treatment runs with glucose-containing fluid alongside insulin.

source.title: The management of diabetic ketoacidosis in adults
source.publisher: Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care

modules.title: Paediatric shock: 10 mL/kg, then reassess

bullets.text: Bolus 10 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid, then reassess before the next one
Reassess after every bolus: heart rate, perfusion, conscious level, liver edge
Look for crackles, a new gallop or an enlarging liver — signs of fluid overload
In DKA and severe malnutrition the approach is different — follow those pathways
If shock persists after 40 to 60 mL/kg, think inotropes and critical care, not more fluid
Weight: use the child's actual weight if known, otherwise an age-based formula

deep_dive.heading: Why the volume changed
points: Practice moved away from routine 20 mL/kg boluses towards smaller volumes with reassessment
The concern is fluid overload and delayed recognition of the child who needs vasoactive support
The reassessment matters more than the number — a bolus given without review is the real error
Get the vasoactive drug conversation started early rather than after the fourth bolus

quiz.question: A 4-year-old with septic shock remains tachycardic and poorly perfused after 40 mL/kg of crystalloid. What is the priority?
options: Another 20 mL/kg bolus
Start vasoactive support and involve critical care
Wait for the lactate to return
Change to colloid
quiz.explanation: Persisting shock after substantial fluid should prompt vasoactive support and critical care involvement rather than continued escalating boluses.

source.title: Sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management (NG51)

modules.title: Fever under 3 months: the ones you do not send home

bullets.text: Under 3 months with fever 38°C or above is a red flag in its own right
Serious bacterial infection can present with no localising signs at all
The traffic light system does not apply below 3 months in the usual way
Hypothermia in a neonate is as concerning as fever
A well-looking baby who fed poorly overnight still needs a senior review
Document the parental concern — it is a recognised risk marker

deep_dive.heading: At the whiteboard
points: Ask what has changed at home: feeding, wet nappies, tone, colour, cry
Check the observations against age-specific ranges, not adult intuition
Follow the local neonatal sepsis pathway for investigations and antibiotic timing
If you are discharging any infant under 3 months, that decision is a senior one

quiz.question: A 6-week-old has a temperature of 38.2°C, is feeding normally and looks well. What is the correct approach?
options: Discharge with safety-net advice
Follow the under-3-month febrile infant pathway with senior involvement
Oral antibiotics and GP review
Reassure — the traffic light system says green
quiz.explanation: Age under 3 months with fever is a high-risk feature regardless of appearance. Local febrile infant pathways and senior review apply.

source.title: Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management (NG143)

modules.title: Aortic dissection: the presentations that look like something else

bullets.text: Pain is often abrupt and maximal at onset rather than crescendo
Beware the stroke, limb ischaemia or syncope with chest or back pain
A normal chest X-ray and a normal D-dimer do not exclude it
Inferior ST elevation can be dissection involving the right coronary ostium
Ask about pulse and blood pressure differences, but their absence proves nothing
If you are seriously considering it, the test is a CT aortogram

deep_dive.heading: The trap worth naming
points: Anticoagulating a dissection as an ACS is the classic catastrophic error
Malperfusion syndromes explain the odd neurological or abdominal presentation
Control heart rate and blood pressure once suspected, and discuss with vascular or cardiothoracics early
Document explicitly why you did or did not image — it is a common complaint theme

quiz.question: A 58-year-old has sudden severe chest pain radiating to the back and a new right hemiparesis. BP differs by 30 mmHg between arms. What is the priority investigation?
options: CT head only
CT aortogram
D-dimer
Bedside echocardiogram alone
quiz.explanation: Sudden chest and back pain with neurological deficit suggests dissection with carotid malperfusion. CT aortogram is the diagnostic test, and thrombolysis would be dangerous.

source.title: RCEMLearning — aortic dissection

modules.title: Thunderclap headache: what the 6-hour CT does and does not do

bullets.text: Non-contrast CT within 6 hours of onset has very high sensitivity for SAH
That performance depends on a modern scanner and a competent reporter
Beyond 6 hours, sensitivity falls and further investigation is needed
LP is timed at 12 hours or more from onset to allow xanthochromia to form
Send CSF for spectrophotometry, and protect the sample from light
Onset time is the anchor for everything — pin it down precisely

deep_dive.heading: The conversation with the patient
points: Explain the residual risk if they decline the LP, and document that discussion
CT angiography is an alternative pathway in some units — know what yours does
A traumatic tap is not a reason to stop thinking; red cell counts alone are unreliable
Consider the alternatives: dissection, venous sinus thrombosis, reversible vasoconstriction

quiz.question: A patient presents 9 hours after a thunderclap headache. Non-contrast CT head is normal. What is appropriate?
options: Discharge — a normal CT excludes SAH
Immediate LP now
Plan LP at 12 hours or more from headache onset, or an agreed local alternative pathway
Repeat CT at 24 hours
quiz.explanation: Beyond 6 hours a normal CT does not exclude SAH. LP is timed at 12 hours or more from onset so xanthochromia can be detected, unless your unit uses a CTA-based pathway.

source.title: RCEMLearning — subarachnoid haemorrhage

modules.title: Paracetamol overdose: the questions that change management

bullets.text: Single time of ingestion, or staggered over more than an hour? It changes everything
The UK uses a single treatment line on the nomogram at 4 hours post-ingestion
Levels before 4 hours cannot be interpreted on the nomogram
Staggered and unknown-time overdoses are treated without waiting for a level
Check TOXBASE for the current regimen — it has changed more than once
Do not stop acetylcysteine for a rash alone; treat and continue

deep_dive.heading: Before the patient leaves
points: End-of-treatment bloods matter: ALT, INR, creatinine and a paracetamol level
Rising ALT or INR means continuing treatment and a liver unit conversation
Every overdose gets a mental health assessment and a capacity-aware risk discussion
Ask about co-ingestants, and about what the patient expected to happen

quiz.question: A patient took paracetamol in unknown amounts over about 8 hours. What is the correct approach?
options: Wait for a 4-hour level
Treat as a staggered overdose without waiting for a level, per TOXBASE
Plot the level on the nomogram from the first tablet
Discharge if asymptomatic
quiz.explanation: The nomogram only applies to a single ingestion at a known time. Staggered overdoses are managed on the TOXBASE pathway without relying on a plotted level.

source.title: TOXBASE (NPIS) — paracetamol

modules.title: Head injury: the anticoagulated patient and the 'minor' bang

bullets.text: Anticoagulation changes the threshold for imaging even without other risk factors
Ask what they are on: DOAC, warfarin, antiplatelet — they are not equivalent
Falls in older people are frequently under-triaged as minor
Reduced GCS with no history is a head injury until proven otherwise
Know your reversal pathway and where the agents are kept before you need them
Discharge advice must be given to someone who will actually be with the patient

deep_dive.heading: Things that get missed
points: The mechanism was not trivial if the patient could not protect themselves on the way down
Consider why they fell — syncope, arrhythmia, sepsis, medication
Chronic subdural presents as confusion or unsteadiness weeks later, not as a headache
Check the C-spine properly in the older patient; injuries there are commonly missed

quiz.question: An 82-year-old on apixaban had an unwitnessed fall, hit her head, and is fully alert with no focal deficit. What is the appropriate action?
options: Discharge with head injury advice
CT head in line with the anticoagulated head injury pathway
Observe for 4 hours then discharge
Skull X-ray
quiz.explanation: Anticoagulation lowers the imaging threshold in head injury. A normal GCS does not exclude significant intracranial bleeding in this group.

source.title: Head injury: assessment and early management (NG232)

modules.title: Testicular torsion: the clock started before they arrived

bullets.text: Acute scrotal pain in a young male is torsion until surgically excluded
Salvage rates fall steeply with time from onset of pain
Abdominal or groin pain with no scrotal complaint still needs the testes examined
Ultrasound must never delay a surgical opinion
Intermittent pain that has settled is still a torsion story
Document the examination, including that you examined at all

deep_dive.heading: Why this keeps appearing in claims
points: Pain referred to the abdomen leads to the genitalia never being examined
A normal-looking scrotum early on gives false reassurance
Waiting for a scan out of hours is a recurring cause of delay
Adolescents may not volunteer the symptom — ask directly and offer a chaperone

quiz.question: A 14-year-old has 3 hours of lower abdominal pain and vomiting. What must be part of the assessment?
options: Urine dip only
Examination of the testes
Abdominal X-ray
Discharge with a surgical review in the morning
quiz.explanation: Torsion frequently presents as abdominal pain. Failure to examine the testes in a boy with abdominal pain is a well-documented cause of delayed diagnosis.

source.title: RCEMLearning — testicular torsion

modules.title: Preoxygenation: the three minutes that decide how the RSI goes

bullets.text: Sit the patient up unless there is a specific reason not to
A well-sealed mask matters more than the flow rate on the flowmeter
Nasal cannulae left on during laryngoscopy extend safe apnoea time
The shocked and acidotic patient desaturates fast — plan for it, don't be surprised
Say the plan aloud: who does what, and what happens if the first look fails
Have push-dose vasopressor drawn up before induction, not after

deep_dive.heading: The 60 seconds before you push drugs
steps: Position: ear to sternal notch, head up
Preoxygenate with a tight seal and add nasal oxygen underneath
Optimise haemodynamics first — fluid or vasopressor before induction
State the plan A, B, C out loud and name who does each
Confirm suction is working and within reach of the intubator
Confirm the failed-airway equipment is open and the person who will use it knows

quiz.question: Which intervention most reliably prolongs safe apnoea time during laryngoscopy?
options: Increasing the tidal volume of bag-mask breaths
Leaving nasal cannula oxygen running through the apnoeic period
Using a smaller tube
Reducing the induction agent dose
quiz.explanation: Apnoeic oxygenation via nasal cannulae maintained through laryngoscopy extends the time to desaturation, particularly in patients with limited reserve.

source.title: Guidelines for the management of tracheal intubation in critically ill adults
source.publisher: Difficult Airway Society / FICM / ICS / RCoA

modules.title: Limping child: don't miss the serious diagnoses

bullets.text: A limp in a child is septic arthritis, Perthes', SUFE, or malignancy until excluded
A child who walks with a limp must be imaged — 'growing pains' is a diagnosis of exclusion
SUFE is easily missed: child aged >9 years with hip pain or restricted movement is high risk
Red flags: age <3 yr, unable to weight bear, fever, systemically unwell, lymphadenopathy, night pain, symptoms >6 weeks
Use the Trust paediatric limping child pathway on the intranet — it has a clear flowchart
Always discuss with a senior before discharging a limping child without imaging

deep_dive.heading: Assessment approach
steps: Full history: duration, fever, systemic symptoms, weight loss, trauma
Examine the hip first — SUFE and Perthes' often present as knee or thigh pain
Look for restricted internal rotation of the hip — a key early sign of SUFE
Check for red flags: if any are present, image and involve senior
Pelvic X-ray for SUFE: subtle widening of physis, Klein's line, frog-leg lateral view
If imaging negative but red flags present, consider USS, MRI, or orthopaedic review

quiz.question: An 11-year-old girl has a 5-week limp. She is otherwise well. What is the single most important next step?
options: Discharge with growing pains diagnosis and GP follow-up
Pelvic X-ray and senior review — SUFE must be excluded
USS hip only — X-ray is not indicated
Physiotherapy referral
quiz.explanation: SUFE is the diagnosis not to miss in a child over 9 with hip symptoms. A pelvic X-ray and senior review are mandatory. This case from Risky Business Ed 44 shows the consequence of discharge without imaging — delayed SUFE with avascular necrosis risk.

source.title: Risky Business — Edition 44 (BHH ED Learning Newsletter, April 2026)

modules.title: Unexplained confusion: don't forget ammonia

bullets.text: Include plasma ammonia in bloods for any adult with confusion, altered consciousness or behavioural change of uncertain cause
Levels >50 µmol/L are hyperammonaemia; >200 µmol/L causes seizures, cerebral oedema, coma, and death
Sample on ice, urgent lab communication — avoid false readings from delayed processing
OTC (ornithine transcarbamylase) deficiency can present in adult females under stress — look like intoxication or psychiatric illness
For ammonia >100–200 µmol/L, urgently involve metabolic/inherited disease specialists per BIMDG protocols
Hyperammonaemia encephalopathy is reversible if caught early — don't miss the window

deep_dive.heading: OTC deficiency — the trap for female patients

points.text: OTC deficiency is the commonest urea cycle disorder — X-linked, so female carriers often undiagnosed
Precipitants in adults: infection, high protein intake, labour, sodium valproate, steroids
Presents as confusion, behavioural change, psychiatric symptoms, or coma — frequently misattributed
Emergency management: high-glucose IV fluids, protein restriction, nitrogen scavengers (sodium benzoate or phenylbutyrate)
Even borderline elevations with clinical suspicion warrant urgent metabolic referral

quiz.question: A 38-year-old woman presents post-partum with confusion and agitation. No obvious infective source. Which test is most likely to reveal the diagnosis?
options: Serum lactate
Plasma ammonia
Urine toxicology screen
Serum cortisol
quiz.explanation: OTC deficiency can present in female carriers post-partum as labour is a recognised precipitant. Plasma ammonia is the key test. This is a diagnosis that is frequently missed — it presents like intoxication or functional illness.

source.title: Risky Business — Edition 44 (BHH ED Learning Newsletter, April 2026)

modules.title: Hand puncture wounds: small entry, serious injury

bullets.text: Small entry wounds can penetrate tendons, nerves and joint capsules — size does not predict depth
Test FDS and FDP in isolation: FDP — hold all other fingers extended and flex the DIP; FDS — hold adjacent fingers extended and flex the PIP
A partially divided tendon may still move — pain on active motion or reduced power is the sign
Altered sensation = nerve injury until excluded by thorough assessment or specialist review
Document explicitly: circulation, sensation, movement of every digit — even if all normal
If the wound cannot be adequately explored in your setting, refer for formal surgical exploration

deep_dive.heading: Hand injury examination sequence
steps: Circulation: capillary refill, radial and ulnar pulses, Allen's test if relevant
Sensation: radial and ulnar digital nerves each finger — light touch and 2-point discrimination
FDP (profundus): stabilise MCP and PIP, ask patient to flex DIP — tests deep flexor
FDS (superficialis): hold all other fingers in extension, ask patient to flex PIP of tested finger
Document power grade and any pain on active motion — partial division causes pain not weakness
Explore the wound base: visualise tendon at full range of motion, not just neutral position

quiz.question: A patient has a puncture wound to the palm. They can flex all fingers. Sensation is intact. What is the safest next step?
options: Discharge — movement is preserved so tendon injury is excluded
Document normal examination and refer for orthopaedic review regardless
Systematically test FDS and FDP in isolation and document power and pain, then decide on referral
X-ray only and discharge if no fracture
quiz.explanation: Preserved movement does not exclude partial tendon division. FDS and FDP must each be tested in isolation. Pain on active motion with preserved movement is the hallmark of a partial cut. This case from Risky Business Ed 44 resulted in a missed flexor tendon rupture and digital nerve injury.

source.title: Risky Business — Edition 44 (BHH ED Learning Newsletter, April 2026)

modules.title: Confirmation bias: don't ever forget glucose

bullets.text: Check a CBG on every diabetic patient — a normal pre-hospital reading hours ago is not sufficient
Pancreatitis + T1DM = always check glucose: DKA and pancreatitis co-exist and each can precipitate the other
Ensure the patient's regular insulin is prescribed — this is not automatically the medical team's job
Confirmation bias: a convincing alternative diagnosis makes you less likely to look for other pathology
Patients in ED for >2 hours need glucose re-monitoring if diabetic — not just on arrival
See the RCEM Time-Critical Medications Safety Flash — insulin is a time-critical drug

points.text: Confirmation bias: you find what you're looking for and stop looking. Classic in pancreatitis, UTI, and 'collapse — found on floor'
The antidote is structured: What else could explain this presentation? What would I do if the obvious diagnosis were wrong?
For any T1DM or T2DM patient: CBG on assessment, CBG on review, insulin prescribed, glucose-containing fluids if BG falling on insulin
DKA in euglycaemia: SGLT-2 inhibitors cause DKA with near-normal glucose — always check ketones in diabetics on flozins
Post-hypoglycaemia monitoring: BM every 15 min if BM <4 mmol/L until stable — document planned frequency

quiz.question: A known T1DM patient presents with epigastric pain typical of their previous pancreatitis episodes. Ambulance BM was 5.2 mmol/L four hours ago. What must not be missed?
options: Nothing — the normal pre-hospital BM excludes DKA
A repeat CBG now and blood ketones, regardless of the previous result
An amylase only — pancreatitis is the working diagnosis
An HbA1c
quiz.explanation: A normal BM four hours ago does not exclude DKA developing subsequently. This case from Risky Business Ed 44 resulted in a missed DKA in a T1DM patient with pancreatitis. The patient went 12 hours without a CBG. Always check glucose on assessment regardless of pre-hospital readings.

source.title: Risky Business — Edition 44 (BHH ED Learning Newsletter, April 2026)

modules.title: Ectopic pregnancy: the positive test that was not escalated

bullets.text: Any female of childbearing age with abdominal pain must have a urine pregnancy test — regardless of what the patient says
A positive result documented in PICS is not enough: it must be verbally escalated to the reviewing clinician
The reviewing clinician must check all outstanding results before making a management plan
Rectal bleeding can be a rare presentation of ectopic pregnancy — tubal erosion into bowel
Always take a full menstrual history: LMP, regularity, intermenstrual bleeding, previous pregnancies
If presentation is atypical but test is positive, discuss with O&G — this is a never-event if missed

deep_dive.heading: From this case (Risky Business Ed 44, BHH)

points.text: Patient: 35F, suprapubic pain and rectal bleeding. Admitted under surgery for lower GI bleed
Urine HCG taken at triage, documented in PICS as positive — never escalated to the clinical team
Three days later: hypotensive collapse on the ward → ruptured ectopic confirmed on TVUSS
The reviewing clinician documented in PICS one hour after the positive test without checking results
Learning: results in PICS do not transfer — verbal escalation of positive pregnancy tests is mandatory

quiz.question: A 35-year-old woman presents with rectal bleeding. A urine pregnancy test taken by nursing at triage is positive in PICS. She denies the possibility of pregnancy. What is the correct action?
options: Accept the patient's history — a positive test with rectal bleeding is almost certainly a false positive
Escalate the positive test verbally to the clinical team and factor it into the assessment
Repeat the test — one positive result is insufficient
Discharge with GP follow-up as presentation is not typical of ectopic
quiz.explanation: This is the exact scenario from a real BHH case. The positive test was not escalated verbally, leading to a delayed diagnosis of ruptured ectopic. A positive pregnancy test must always be verbally communicated and change the working diagnosis, regardless of patient history.

source.title: Risky Business — Edition 44 (BHH ED Learning Newsletter, April 2026)

modules.title: Hypoglycaemia: treatment is not the end of the job

bullets.text: After treating hypoglycaemia: BM every 15 minutes until stable if BM was <4 mmol/L
A corrected BM does not mean the episode is over — rebound hypoglycaemia is common with long-acting insulin or sulphonylureas
Document planned BM monitoring frequency in your clinical notes
Analgesia delays in patients with pain can contribute to agitation, absconding, and missed diagnoses
Adequate analgesia within 15 minutes of arrival for moderate (score 4–6) and severe pain (score ≥7) is the RCEM standard
Consider capacity documentation for high-risk patients at risk of self-discharge before clerking is complete

deep_dive.heading: From the Risky Business Ed 44 case

points.text: Patient: 47M, found unresponsive at home post self-discharge. BM 0.7, GCS 3. Cardiac arrest at BM 0.61 at 05:09
Post-treatment BMs: 02:34 BM=27.3, 02:47 BM=10.8, then 05:09 BM=0.61 → cardiac arrest
2+ hour gap in BM monitoring after initial correction — no frequency documented in plan
Key learning: treat the hypoglycaemia, document the monitoring plan, and do not let BM monitoring intervals extend
Also: inadequately treated pain contributed to self-discharge before full assessment — analgesia is time-critical

quiz.question: You have treated a patient with symptomatic hypoglycaemia (BM 2.1). After IV dextrose the BM is 7.4. What is the correct next step?
options: Discharge once BM is above 4
BM every 15 minutes until stable, document planned monitoring frequency, check cause and insulin doses
Single repeat BM in 1 hour is sufficient
Hand over to nursing without specific monitoring instructions
quiz.explanation: A corrected BM does not end the clinical responsibility. Post-hypoglycaemia protocol: BM every 15 minutes if BM was <4 mmol/L. Document the planned monitoring frequency. Check for precipitating cause and whether insulin needs adjustment. This case resulted in a cardiac arrest from rebound hypoglycaemia.

source.title: Risky Business — Edition 44 (BHH ED Learning Newsletter, April 2026)

modules.title: Oxygen prescribing in COPD: the PICS default trap

bullets.text: COPD patients: prescribe oxygen as PRN with target SpO2 88–92% on PICS — not as regular 4× daily
If oxygen is removed from PICS by another team, PICS defaults to Scale 1 (SpO2 >94%) — dangerous in COPD
If you cancel or modify an oxygen prescription, re-prescribe it correctly immediately
Nursing staff must escalate to a clinician if oxygen is being administered without a prescription
Type 2 respiratory failure risk: SpO2 target >94% in COPD can suppress hypoxic drive → CO2 retention → acidosis → NIV
If in doubt, use the BTS oxygen prescribing guidelines and target SpO2 88–92% in all known COPD patients

points.text: COPD patient prescribed Scale 2 oxygen (88–92%) in ED → referred to medical team
Medical SHO cancels oxygen prescription → PICS defaults to Scale 1 (>94%)
Nursing staff commence oxygen when SpO2 falls below 94% as prompted by PICS
Patient develops type 2 respiratory failure over hours → CO2 narcosis → near-NIV
Systems issue: PICS should not default COPD/type 2 RF patients to Scale 1 when oxygen is removed — raised with IT
Clinical issue: anyone cancelling oxygen in a COPD patient must re-prescribe PRN with correct target immediately

quiz.question: A known COPD patient is on Scale 2 oxygen (SpO2 88–92%) in ED. The medical SHO clerking them cancels the oxygen prescription. What should happen next?
options: Nothing — the patient will be monitored by nursing
The SHO must immediately re-prescribe oxygen as PRN with SpO2 target 88–92%
Scale 1 oxygen (>94%) is acceptable as a default
Oxygen only needs re-prescribing if SpO2 falls below 85%
quiz.explanation: Cancelling oxygen without re-prescribing causes PICS to default to Scale 1, which is dangerous in COPD. The prescriber must immediately re-prescribe PRN oxygen with target SpO2 88–92%. This is a real BHH incident from Risky Business Ed 44 — the patient developed type 2 respiratory failure as a direct consequence.

source.title: Risky Business — Edition 44 (BHH ED Learning Newsletter, April 2026)

modules.title: Sickle cell crisis: always read the care plan, always treat the pain

bullets.text: When a sickle cell patient presents in crisis, read their haematology care plan letter immediately — it contains their individual protocol
NICE: give opioids early for severe pain — oral morphine for moderate, IV or SC for severe
Analgesia within 30 minutes of arrival for pain score ≥7 — this is an RCEM quality indicator
Reassess pain continuously — inadequate analgesia leads to distress, longer admissions and loss of trust
Add paracetamol and NSAIDs (if not contraindicated) as adjuncts — multimodal is the NICE standard
Monitor for respiratory depression if high-dose opioids used; escalate if pain uncontrolled despite protocol

deep_dive.heading: Why sickle cell pain is undertreated

points.text: Unconscious bias and stigma around opioid-seeking behaviour — studies consistently show sickle cell patients wait longer for analgesia than other painful conditions
Each patient's pain threshold and treatment dose differs — the care plan exists because one-size does not fit all
Hydration, warmth and anxiolysis are important adjuncts but do not replace analgesia
Haematology team can advise on hydroxycarbamide, blood transfusion and acute chest syndrome risk
Acute chest syndrome: new chest pain, fever and hypoxia in sickle cell = medical emergency

quiz.question: A sickle cell patient presents in crisis with pain score 9. They hand you their haematology care plan letter. What is the single most important first step?
options: Give standard analgesia per your usual protocol and review the letter later
Read the care plan letter and prescribe analgesia per the individual protocol — do not delay
Contact haematology before giving any opioids
Give paracetamol and ibuprofen first and escalate if no response
quiz.explanation: The haematology care plan contains the patient's individual protocol including specific doses. Reading it immediately and prescribing per the plan is the correct approach. A real BHH case (Risky Business Ed 44) showed a patient with pain score consistently >8 who did not receive adequate analgesia despite multiple nursing prompts.

source.title: Risky Business — Edition 44 (BHH ED Learning Newsletter, April 2026)

modules.title: Glass lacerations: always image before you close

bullets.text: Always X-ray wounds caused by glass, ceramic, or brittle materials before closure — even if the wound appears clean
Glass is radio-opaque — plain X-ray will detect fragments ≥2 mm; smaller fragments may need CT or USS
Explore the wound base and visualise to its deepest point before closure — do not close if you cannot see the bottom
Document: mechanism (glass/ceramic), exploration findings, whether imaging was performed and result
If imaging is deemed unnecessary, document your reasoning — this is your defence if a fragment is later found
A cleaned and closed wound does not exclude a retained foreign body — the patient presenting 2 weeks later is a common scenario

points.text: Patient: glass laceration cleaned and closed without imaging. Re-presented 2 weeks later with persistent wound pain
X-ray revealed an 18 mm glass fragment — required surgical removal
Key failure: no imaging before closure despite glass mechanism
Glass X-ray: window glass, beer glass and ceramic are reliably seen on plain film; car windscreen glass is less radio-opaque — lower threshold for CT
USS is useful for non-radio-opaque foreign bodies (wood, plastic) and is operator-dependent

quiz.question: A patient has a 1 cm laceration from breaking a glass. The wound appears clean and superficial. What must be done before closure?
options: Close the wound — it appears superficial and clean
X-ray the wound to exclude retained glass fragment, then explore and close
USS only if clinical suspicion is high
No imaging needed for lacerations under 2 cm
quiz.explanation: Glass mechanism mandates X-ray before closure regardless of wound appearance. An 18 mm fragment was missed in the real Risky Business Ed 44 case because imaging was not done before a wound that appeared clean and superficial was closed.

source.title: Risky Business — Edition 44 (BHH ED Learning Newsletter, April 2026)
